title: RPC guards testify on first day of inquest into inmate's death in 2019
subtitle: Two correctional officers who discovered Benjamin Toutsaint unresponsive on May 18, 2019 testified on the first day of a coroner's inquest.
article: A correctional officer who was one of the first people to find Benjamin Toutsaint unresponsive in his cell at the federal Regional Psychiatric Centre in Saskatoon an inquest jury he did not believe they were going to lose the 32-year-old that day.
Efforts to revive Toutsaint were unsuccessful and he was pronounced dead on May 18, 2019. He is believed to have died of suicide in his cell in the facility's Bow unit.
He had been serving a two-year sentence for assault since Oct. 25, 2018.

An inquest is a fact-finding, not fault-finding, process that establishes when and how someone died. It may also highlight dangerous conditions or practices, and the jury can make non-binding recommendations to prevent future deaths.
The inquest is expected to last until Wednesday and hear from eight witnesses.
Correctional officer Ryan Chiesa, who was working the day shift, testified that he was not told Toutsaint may have been suicidal, but would have appreciated receiving that information.
He said he saw Toutsaint standing in the middle of his cell, and perhaps pacing, around 4:30 p.m.
During the 5 p.m. count, the guards were told their count of a unit was short by one, the inquest heard. During the recount, guards discovered an unresponsive Toutsaint.

Chiesa said Toutsaint had managed to use a ligature threaded behind a flat metal bar mounted to a wall that belonged to a ligature-proof coat hook. He questioned whether the coat hooks need to be in the cells.
A second guard, Chris Crosby, said he ran to get a 911 tool that can be used to cut through ligatures. The tools are in the unit, but guards do not carry them.

After freeing Toutsaint, Chiesa said the guards took him out of the cell to administer CPR and First Aid, and an AED was brought over. Chiesa said he was still doing chest compressions when EMTs arrived.
"I didn't think he was deceased at the time we cut him down," he said. "I didn't think that we were going to lose him."

Crosby suggested that "suspension points" - which could be used for ligatures - should be removed from all cells. The in-cell coat hooks are designed to buckle, but Crosby said Toutsaint circumvented that. He thinks "bed boards" - clipboards with lists of inmates' cell assignments - should be used during formal counts to reduce recounts, he added.
He said Toutsaint was not breathing when he cut him down.

Assistant warden Grace Chopty told the inquest the health and security sides of the institution communicate frequently and there is a process the institution would have to go through to have the hooks removed.
At the direction of Chief Coroner Clive Weighill, jurors for the inquest were drawn from two pools to ensure Indigenous representation.
Members of Toutsaint's family attended the inquest on Monday and have standing to question witnesses.
